contents.text: A metaphor compares two things that are not alike. Plato used a metaphor to compare a sailing ship to a democracy.

In his metaphor, the sailors argue with each other about subjects they know nothing about. In a democracy, Plato believed that people are allowed to have power on issues they know nothing about. Like the sailors in his metaphor, Plato thought that Athenians refused to believe that anyone else knew more than they did about government.

contents.text: A metaphor compares two things that are not alike. Plato used a metaphor to compare a sailing ship to a democracy.

In his metaphor, the sailors argue with each other about subjects they know nothing about. In a democracy, Plato believed that people are allowed to have power on issues they know nothing about. Like the sailors in his metaphor, Plato thought that Athenians refused to believe that anyone else knew more than they did about government.

header.text: The number of city-states in ancient Greece changed, but at times there were as many as 1,000 city-states! Each city-state had its own government, economy, and culture, but they did have some things in common. Read the passage about Greek city-states. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: All Greek people spoke the same language. Sharing a language allowed ancient Greeks to spread ideas between city-states. For example, city-states shared the same Greek gods, goddesses, and religious festivals. City-states also came together to compete in the Olympic Games, which began in 776 BCE.

Athens and Sparta are two of the most famous Greek city-states. Many historians give Athenians credit for inventing philosophy and democracy. Athenians also developed a style of art and architecture that has been copied for centuries. In comparison, historians remember Spartans for developing military strategies later civilizations adopted. The Spartan leader Lycurgus is given credit for establishing law and order in Sparta as well as granting equality to all citizens. Even though Athens was a democracy, Athenian citizens were treated differently based on their social group.

Although city-states such as Athens could trade for food, Sparta was surrounded by mountains that made trade difficult. So, the Spartans relied on agriculture. The ancient Greek historian Pausanias (paw-SA-nee-uhs) described the role of

header.text: The number of city-states in ancient Greece changed, but at times there were as many as 1,000 city-states! Each city-state had its own government, economy, and culture, but they did have some things in common. Read the passage about Greek city-states. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: All Greek people spoke the same language. Sharing a language allowed ancient Greeks to spread ideas between city-states. For example, city-states shared the same Greek gods, goddesses, and religious festivals. City-states also came together to compete in the Olympic Games, which began in 776 BCE.

Athens and Sparta are two of the most famous Greek city-states. Many historians give Athenians credit for inventing philosophy and democracy. Athenians also developed a style of art and architecture that has been copied for centuries. In comparison, historians remember Spartans for developing military strategies later civilizations adopted. The Spartan leader Lycurgus is given credit for establishing law and order in Sparta as well as granting equality to all citizens. Even though Athens was a democracy, Athenian citizens were treated differently based on their social group.

header.text: The number of city-states in ancient Greece changed, but at times there were as many as 1,000 city-states! Each city-state had its own government, economy, and culture, but they did have some things in common. Read the passage about Greek city-states. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: All Greek people spoke the same language. Sharing a language allowed ancient Greeks to spread ideas between city-states. For example, city-states shared the same Greek gods, goddesses, and religious festivals. City-states also came together to compete in the Olympic Games, which began in 776 BCE.

Athens and Sparta are two of the most famous Greek city-states. Many historians give Athenians credit for inventing philosophy and democracy. Athenians also developed a style of art and architecture that has been copied for centuries. In comparison, historians remember Spartans for developing military strategies later civilizations adopted. The Spartan leader Lycurgus is given credit for establishing law and order in Sparta as well as granting equality to all citizens. Even though Athens was a democracy, Athenian citizens were treated differently based on their social group.

header.text: Each Greek city-state had different rules and expectations for citizenship. Read about citizenship in Athens and Sparta. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: In ancient Athens, only men could be citizens. Men became citizens when they turned 18. At that time, they were required to serve in the military and in government. All citizens also had to attend assembly meetings to vote on laws. If there were not at least 6,000 citizens present, enslaved people would go and find citizens to bring them to the assembly. Any citizen over 30 could be randomly selected to serve on the council of 500 for a year. The council of 500 met daily to work on laws. Athenian citizens were also randomly chosen to serve on juries of sometimes 500 or 1,000 people

Only Spartan men could be citizens. Citizenship in Sparta was earned. Men in their 20s competed to show their strength and earn the right to be citizens. Then they had to give back to Sparta through military service. When the council of elders decided that Sparta needed to go to war, Spartan men between 20 and 60 years old would be called up for battle. Unlike Athenians, most Spartans did not want to be politicians, and they were not required to be involved in politics. Spartan men over 30 could decide whether or not to go to the assembly and vote on laws.

header.text: Each Greek city-state had different rules and expectations for citizenship. Read about citizenship in Athens and Sparta. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: In ancient Athens, only men could be citizens. Men became citizens when they turned 18. At that time, they were required to serve in the military and in government. All citizens also had to attend assembly meetings to vote on laws. If there were not at least 6,000 citizens present, enslaved people would go and find citizens to bring them to the assembly. Any citizen over 30 could be randomly selected to serve on the council of 500 for a year. The council of 500 met daily to work on laws. Athenian citizens were also randomly chosen to serve on juries of sometimes 500 or 1,000 people

Only Spartan men could be citizens. Citizenship in Sparta was earned. Men in their 20s competed to show their strength and earn the right to be citizens. Then they had to give back to Sparta through military service. When the council of elders decided that Sparta needed to go to war, Spartan men between 20 and 60 years old would be called up for battle. Unlike Athenians, most Spartans did not want to be politicians, and they were not required to be involved in politics. Spartan men over 30 could decide whether or not to go to the assembly and vote on laws.

Any citizen over 30 could be randomly selected to serve on the council of 500 for a year. The council of 500 met daily to work on laws. Athenian citizens were also randomly chosen to serve on juries of sometimes 500 or 1,000 people

Only Spartan men could be citizens. Citizenship in Sparta was earned. Men in their 20s competed to show their strength and earn the right to be citizens. Then they had to give back to Sparta through military service. When the council of elders decided that Sparta needed to go to war, Spartan men between 20 and 60 years old would be called up for battle. Unlike Athenians, most Spartans did not want to be politicians, and they were not required to be involved in politics. Spartan men over 30 could decide whether or not to go to the assembly and vote on laws.

header.text: Each Greek city-state had different rules and expectations for citizenship. Read about citizenship in Athens and Sparta. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: In ancient Athens, only men could be citizens. Men became citizens when they turned 18. At that time, they were required to serve in the military and in government. All citizens also had to attend assembly meetings to vote on laws. If there were not at least 6,000 citizens present, enslaved people would go and find citizens to bring them to the assembly. Any citizen over 30 could be randomly selected to serve on the council of 500 for a year. The council of 500 met daily to work on laws. Athenian citizens were also randomly chosen to serve on juries of sometimes 500 or 1,000 people

Only Spartan men could be citizens. Citizenship in Sparta was earned. Men in their 20s competed to show their strength and earn the right to be citizens. Then they had to give back to Sparta through military service. When the council of elders decided that Sparta needed to go to war, Spartan men between 20 and 60 years old would be called up for battle. Unlike Athenians, most Spartans did not want to be politicians, and they were not required to be involved in politics. Spartan men over 30 could decide whether or not to go to the assembly and vote on laws.

elements.text: In Athens, boys learned about many subjects, including how to debate, write laws, and fight in the military. Athenian girls were not educated in schools but were taught how to do chores.
In Sparta, there were not many politicians, so boys were prepared for the military. Spartan girls were also expected to be strong and had more opportunities than girls in Athens.

header.text: Read the text from one ancient historian about Philip II's assassination. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Pausanias, Philip II's bodyguard, had been treated unfairly by Philip II's relatives. Philip II refused to do anything, so Pausanias killed him. Most of the blame for the murder fell on Olympias for encouraging Pausanias in his anger and even urging him to get his revenge. But some of the blame was on Alexander, too. Some people said that Pausanias complained to Alexander, who told Pausanias to kill Philip II and his relatives.
<citation>Adapted from Plutarch, Parallel Lives</citation>

. Each city-state consisted of a city and its surrounding land, and each had its own government. Read the passage about relations between Macedonia and the Greek city-states. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: People who were struggling to get by, like

(as-CAN-ee-us), were attracted to early Rome because the city gave them new opportunities to improve their lives. In older cities, those who were not born into wealthy families were rarely able to get ahead.
People who had a bad reputation in their old community, like
(lay-ON-tuh-cus), would have had a chance to start over in early Rome. The growing community needed anyone who was able to help defend the city, grow crops, or build buildings!

header.text: These people would probably not move to early Rome:

pieces.text: A prince like

(noo-MAY-see) probably would not move to early Rome, because it was not yet an important city. Etruscan princes would want to live in wealthier, larger, and older cities so they could be around other powerful princes or kings.

header.text: Over time, historians have had different ideas about how Rome changed from a monarchy to republic. The first passage summarizes writings from an ancient author living hundreds of years after the end of the monarchy. The second passage was written by a historian in the last 50 years. Look at each passage. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: After Romans freed their city from the cruel, selfish king, they had to protect it against his angry friends. The king had been the head of the army, the government, the courts, and Roman religion. So Romans had to come together to start choosing their own leaders while they were also under attack from the former king's allies. Suddenly, instead of having nothing to do with politics, Rome's people were now in charge, guided by the wise advice of the Senate.

After getting rid of the king, the people and senators of Rome were forced to govern their city themselves. They often disagreed about who should do what. At first, they arrived at a short-term arrangement, where the Senate came up with ideas and Roman citizens approved or rejected them. Because this kind of government worked well enough, it eventually became a lasting tradition.

header.text: Over time, historians have had different ideas about how Rome changed from a monarchy to republic. The first passage summarizes writings from an ancient author living hundreds of years after the end of the monarchy. The second passage was written by a historian in the last 50 years. Look at each passage. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: After Romans freed their city from the cruel, selfish king, they had to protect it against his angry friends. The king had been the head of the army, the government, the courts, and Roman religion. So Romans had to come together to start choosing their own leaders while they were also under attack from the former king's allies. Suddenly, instead of having nothing to do with politics, Rome's people were now in charge, guided by the wise advice of the Senate.

After getting rid of the king, the people and senators of Rome were forced to govern their city themselves. They often disagreed about who should do what. At first, they arrived at a short-term arrangement, where the Senate came up with ideas and Roman citizens approved or rejected them. Because this kind of government worked well enough, it eventually became a lasting tradition.

table.text: After Romans freed their city from the cruel, selfish king, they had to protect it against his angry friends. The king had been the head of the army, the government, the courts, and Roman religion. So Romans had to come together to start choosing their own leaders while they were also under attack from the former king's allies. Suddenly, instead of having nothing to do with politics, Rome's people were now in charge, guided by the wise advice of the Senate.

After getting rid of the king, the people and senators of Rome were forced to govern their city themselves. They often disagreed about who should do what. At first, they arrived at a short-term arrangement, where the Senate came up with ideas and Roman citizens approved or rejected them. Because this kind of government worked well enough, it eventually became a lasting tradition.

content.text: Augustus had fewer rivals to be the next sole ruler of Roman territory.

explanationText.text: Mark Antony and Caesarion were competing with Augustus for control of Roman territory. After their deaths, Augustus had less competition during his rise to power.

content.text: Augustus was able to gain control of Egypt's wealth to pay his soldiers and pay for building projects.

explanationText.text: Egypt was a wealthy kingdom. After Cleopatra died and Augustus conquered Egypt, Augustus used its wealth to pay his soldiers for their continued service and for building projects in the city of Rome.

content.text: Augustus was able to take Egypt's grain and natural resources and use them to support Romans.

explanationText.text: Romans relied on grain and other goods from Egypt. After Cleopatra died and Augustus had control of Egypt, he could use these resources to help provide food and supplies for Rome.

content.text: Augustus was able to marry Cleopatra to become the new pharaoh of Egypt.

explanationText.text: Augustus never married Cleopatra. She took her own life to avoid being taken prisoner by Augustus.

In this skill, you are going to learn about the Byzantine Empire. The history of the Byzantine Empire starts in 312 CE, when a man named

became emperor of the Roman Empire. At this time, the Roman Empire controlled all of the land around the Mediterranean Sea. At first, the capital of the Roman Empire was the city of Rome, in present-day Italy. But in 330 CE, Constantine moved the empire's capital to a city in present-day Turkey. He called that city
, which means "The City of Constantine" in Greek.

header.text: When Constantine decided to move the empire's capital, he had to weigh the advantages of both Rome and Constantinople. Look at the map of the Roman Empire. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A map of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa titled "The Roman Empire." Regions controlled by the Roman Empire include the entire northern coast of Africa, the southern half of Europe, and the western coast of Asia, encompassing the entire Turkish peninsula. Rome, located near the western coast in the center of the Italian Peninsula, and Constantinople, located just north of the Turkish peninsula on a small strip of land that divides the Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea, are marked.   Arrows indicate invasions into the Roman Empire. Many of these arrows begin in northwestern Asia: one branches off towards the Turkish peninsula, and the rest pass through the northernmost part of the Roman Empire. Only one of these points towards Constantinople, and one arrow points from Constantinople to Rome (circumnavigating the Adriatic Sea). The other arrows point toward the European region of the Roman Empire, passing though and eventually pointing to Rome. One of these arrows points through present day Spain's Iberian peninsula, across the northern coast of Africa, and finally crosses back through the Mediterranean Sea, pointing towards Rome and the archipelagoes that surround the Italian peninsula.

In this skill, you are going to learn about the Byzantine Empire. The history of the Byzantine Empire starts in 312 CE, when a man named

became emperor of the Roman Empire. At this time, the Roman Empire controlled all of the land around the Mediterranean Sea. At first, the capital of the Roman Empire was the city of Rome, in present-day Italy. But in 330 CE, Constantine moved the empire's capital to a city in present-day Turkey. He called that city
, which means "The City of Constantine" in Greek.

header.text: When Constantine decided to move the empire's capital, he had to weigh the advantages of both Rome and Constantinople. Look at the map of the Roman Empire. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A map of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa titled "The Roman Empire." Regions controlled by the Roman Empire include the entire northern coast of Africa, the southern half of Europe, and the western coast of Asia, encompassing the entire Turkish peninsula. Rome, located near the western coast in the center of the Italian Peninsula, and Constantinople, located just north of the Turkish peninsula on a small strip of land that divides the Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea, are marked.   Arrows indicate invasions into the Roman Empire. Many of these arrows begin in northwestern Asia: one branches off towards the Turkish peninsula, and the rest pass through the northernmost part of the Roman Empire. Only one of these points towards Constantinople, and one arrow points from Constantinople to Rome (circumnavigating the Adriatic Sea). The other arrows point toward the European region of the Roman Empire, passing though and eventually pointing to Rome. One of these arrows points through present day Spain's Iberian peninsula, across the northern coast of Africa, and finally crosses back through the Mediterranean Sea, pointing towards Rome and the archipelagoes that surround the Italian peninsula.

contents.text: Sort the following advantages based on whether they describe Constantinople or Rome.

label.text: The city is located farther away from most invading groups.
The city is located on a tiny strip of land between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean Sea, which made it harder for invading groups to attack by land.
The city is located close to the regions of Greece, Egypt, and Asia, which had the most wealth available for the emperor to use.
The city is located near the center of the Mediterranean Sea, which made it easier to get to places all around the Roman Empire.

by an invading group in 476 CE. But the Eastern Roman Empire was wealthy and had a large military to defend itself, so it remained independent. alternativeText.text: A map of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa titled "The Roman Empire." Regions controlled by the Roman Empire include the entire northern coast of Africa, the southern half of Europe, and the western coast of Asia, encompassing the entire Turkish peninsula. Rome, located near the western coast in the center of the Italian Peninsula, and Constantinople, located just north of the Turkish peninsula on a small strip of land that divides the Mediterranean Sea and Black Sea, are marked.   Arrows indicate invasions into the Roman Empire. Many of these arrows begin in northwestern Asia: one branches off towards the Turkish peninsula, and the rest pass through the northernmost part of the Roman Empire. Only one of these points towards Constantinople, and one arrow points from Constantinople to Rome (circumnavigating the Adriatic Sea). The other arrows point toward the European region of the Roman Empire, passing though and eventually pointing to Rome. One of these arrows points through present day Spain's Iberian peninsula, across the northern coast of Africa, and finally crosses back through the Mediterranean Sea, pointing towards Rome and the archipelagoes that surround the Italian peninsula.
